summary: The first part of a series on privacy enhancement for Internet electronic mail, defining message encipherment and authentication procedures. It is meant to work with many key management approaches, both symmetric and public-key. It came out of IAB Privacy Task Force meetings, was a proposal, and was replaced by RFC 1040 and RFC 1113.

eli5.summary: It explains how to put your email in a locked box and sign it, so only the right person can open it and they know it truly came from you.

questions: how to encrypt and authenticate internet email
subtitle: The first Privacy-Enhanced Mail RFC: end-to-end encryption and sender authentication for Internet email, with no changes to mail relays.

tldr.problem: Internet electronic mail travels through relays in the clear, with no way for a recipient to be sure who sent it, that it was unaltered, or that nobody else read it.
tldr.mechanism: Sender and recipient mail programs encrypt with DES in CBC mode and compute a message authentication code. They wrap the result in a printable encapsulated message with control headers, and protect the per-message key with a longer-lived interchange key.
tldr.outcome: It was a proposed protocol, and key management was left to a later RFC. It was obsoleted by RFC 1040 and RFC 1113.

today: RFC 989 was a proposal, and it was obsoleted by RFC 1040 and then RFC 1113, so it is no longer the current definition of Privacy-Enhanced Mail. Its status is listed as Unknown.

sections.title: Goals, Services and Limits
sections.content:
RFC 989 defines message encipherment and authentication procedures as the first phase of an effort to give Internet electronic mail privacy enhancement services: confidentiality, authentication and message integrity. They are provided by end-to-end cryptography between the originator's and recipient's User Agent processes, with no special processing needed at the Message Transfer System, including intermediate relay sites. A site or a user can therefore adopt the scheme without affecting anyone else.

Two service options are supported. One gives sender authentication and integrity verification. The other adds confidentiality through encryption. There is no confidentiality without authentication. Encryption and authentication can be applied to selected parts of a message.

The RFC also lists what it does not address: access control, traffic flow security, address list accuracy, routing control, serial reuse of PCs by several users, proof of receipt and non-deniability, and automatic matching of acknowledgments to messages. The measures must be implementable at the user agent level or above, rather than inside SMTP servers.
sections.eli5: It protects a letter from the sender's desk to the reader's desk. The post offices in between do not need to know anything special.

sections.title: Two-Level Keys and Message Processing
sections.content:
The design uses a two-level keying hierarchy. Data Encrypting Keys (DEKs) encrypt the message text and compute message authentication codes (MACs). They are generated for each message, so no predistribution is needed. Interchange Keys (IKs) encrypt DEKs for transmission. An IK may be a single symmetric key, or, with asymmetric cryptography, the combination of a public component used by the originator and a secret component used by the recipient. Ordinarily the same IK is used for all messages between an originator and a recipient for a period of time.

Each message carries the DEK and MAC encrypted under an IK for each named recipient, with an identifier (IK ID) that tells the recipient which IK was used. On receipt, the printable encoding is decoded, the text is decrypted if it was encrypted, the MAC is verified, and the canonical text is converted to the recipient's local form.
sections.eli5: Each letter gets its own one-time padlock key. That small key is then locked inside a second box that only the intended reader can open with a key the two people already share.

sections.title: Encryption Algorithms and Modes
sections.content:
Message text encryption and MAC computation use the Block Cipher Algorithm DEA-1, which is equivalent to the Data Encryption Standard (DES), in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode. A unique initializing vector is generated for and sent with each encrypted message. Keys are encrypted under an interchange key using DEA-1 in Electronic Codebook (ECB) mode, with an optional indicator for another mode such as Encrypt-Decrypt-Encrypt (EDE).

Another algorithm may be used if it is a 64-bit block cipher working in 8 octet blocks, can be used in ECB and CBC modes, can be keyed with the RFC's procedures, is appropriate for MAC computation, and has key fields of at most 16 octets. Support for public-key algorithms for key encryption was under consideration, and support for key encryption modes other than ECB is optional.
sections.eli5: The scrambling machine is DES, which works on small chunks and mixes each chunk with the one before it, so patterns in the message do not show.

sections.title: Canonical Form and Printable Encoding
sections.content:
Mail systems differ in character sets and line endings, and SMTP can carry 7-bit characters but not arbitrary 8-bit data. If transport changed even one byte of ciphertext, decryption and MAC checks would fail. So the text goes through four forms: the local form, a canonical form (the ASCII, CR LF inter-SMTP representation of RFC 822), an enciphered form padded with zero-valued octets to a multiple of 8 octets, and a printable form.

The printable encoding takes each 3 octets and writes 4 characters, 6 bits per character, drawn from a 64-character subset of IA5. A final short group is padded with the character =. Lines hold 64 printable characters. An asterisk brackets any part of the message that the sender excluded from encryption and authentication. The scheme is summarized as Encode(Encipher(Canonicalize(Local_Form))).

The character set deliberately leaves out the hyphen character, so encoded text can never be mistaken for an encapsulation boundary line.
sections.eli5: Mail systems only reliably carry plain letters and digits. So the scrambled message is rewritten using only safe characters, a bit like spelling out a secret code in ordinary letters.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Control Fields
sections.content:
The protected message is wrapped using an encapsulation method derived from RFC 934. An ordinary RFC 822 header comes first, and then the encapsulated message sits between two lines reading -----PRIVACY-ENHANCED MESSAGE BOUNDARY-----. After the opening line comes an encapsulated header of control fields, a blank line, and the encoded text. These fields look like RFC 822 headers but are a disjoint set. Sensitive header data such as Subject: should be placed inside the encapsulated text, and the RFC suggests an outer Subject: of "Encrypted Mail Follows".

The control fields are X-Proc-Type (version 1, then A for authentication only or E for authentication plus encryption), X-Pad-Count (0 to 7 padding octets), X-IV (a 64-bit initializing vector as 16 hex digits), X-IK-ID and X-Key-Info. Each X-IK-ID is followed by an X-Key-Info holding the DEK and the MAC encrypted under that IK. For DEA-1 the DEK is 16 hex digits and the MAC is 16 hex digits. Encryption uses a variant of the DEK formed by modulo-2 addition of F0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0.
sections.eli5: The sealed message goes inside a labeled envelope. The labels say how it was locked, which key box to use, and how much filler was added at the end.

sections.title: Interchange Keys, Mailing Lists and Naming
sections.content:
The RFC says the way IKs reach parties is outside its scope; detailed key management was left to a later RFC. An IK is tied to an Issuing Authority. An X-IK-ID holds the Issuing Authority, an IK qualifier and an optional use indicator (ECB or EDE, default ECB), separated by colons. As an interim measure the qualifier takes the form sender/recipient/numid, where names look like user@domain-qualified-host.

For mailing lists there are two methods. With IK-per-list all members share one IK. That is the normal case for remote exploder sites, but it exposes the shared IK, makes revocation difficult, and lets any holder masquerade as another sender. With IK-per-recipient the sender expands the list, encrypting only the small DEK and MAC under each member's IK, so IKs can be revoked individually.

The RFC admits that unique naming of users is unresolved and needs study, including possibly using the Domain Name System. It lists areas for further study: user naming, standardizing Issuing Authority functions, public key algorithms for DEKs, and interoperability with X.400 mail.
sections.eli5: For a club mailing list, either everyone shares one key, which is easy but risky, or the sender locks a small copy of the secret separately for each member, which takes more work but is safer.

items.label: Processing type
items.desc: Version 1, then A (authentication only) or E (authentication and encryption).

items.label: Padding count
items.desc: Number of zero-valued octets added, 0 to 7.

items.label: Initializing vector
items.desc: 64-bit vector as 16 hex digits; used when encrypting.

items.label: Interchange key ID
items.desc: Issuing Authority, IK qualifier and optional use indicator.

items.label: Key information
items.desc: The DEK and the MAC, each encrypted under the IK named just before.
